results.note: The substantive search dates, article/study classifications, drug-row counts and arithmetic are supported. Thirteen randomized trials is written out on p. 4, so the absence of the numeral 13 from a mechanical search is a text-format issue, not a page error. The abstract's 763 is genuinely on p. 1, which the original page range/locator omitted; 761 is explicit on p. 4 and is the sum of all 25 Table 1 row totals (see reader411_arithmetic.json). The explicit 25-study count is also in the abstract. Add Eligibility criteria to the p. 2 locator. The replacement states precisely what is observable: no formal appraisal is reported and no synthesis was planned, rather than asserting an unobservable absence of work or overlooking the descriptive outcome summaries in Table 1/Discussion. The exclusion concerns addiction treatment, not proof that every participant in every primary report had no substance-use history. Role qualifies is appropriate. Potential surrounding-statement effects: retain attribution to this descriptive review; the 25 entries/761 sum do not establish unique independent cohorts or participants, and this review cannot estimate effects of set/setting. This check neither changes nor independently validates the claims' certainty/status ratings.
results.corrected_extracted: Systematic review of clinical trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders, excluding addiction treatment: PubMed and Web of Science searched to 12 September 2022 and rerun on 6 December 2023, with English- or French-language publications eligible. It reports 27 articles grouped into 25 studies, classified as 13 randomized and 12 open-label; Table 1 has 25 study rows, comprising 16 psilocybin, five ayahuasca, two LSD and two labelled DMT. The Results reports 761 participants, and the Table 1 row totals independently sum to 761; the abstract instead reports 763. These are the review's study entries and participant totals, not independently verified counts of distinct trials or people from the primary reports. No review protocol, registration or formal trial quality/risk-of-bias appraisal is reported in the article. Each study was scored for reporting 16 set-and-setting sub-domains; the Methods states that no data synthesis was planned.

results.note: Confirmed against original printed pp. 475–477 (PDF pp. 4–6), read as extracted text and own 150 dpi page renders. Methods > Psilocybin Sessions and Musical Genres, second paragraph (printed p. 476), states that 25% of Western-classical tracks were shared, mainly at the beginning/end; approximately 60 minutes of music selected before the first session was used in all sessions at approximately four hours after dosing, with one participant choosing none. The top of printed p. 476 identifies the subsample as ten, so nine of ten receiving personal music follows arithmetically. Note 22 on printed p. 477 explicitly reports removing three overtone tracks after the first three participants and minor ordering changes. Discussion paragraph 3 on printed p. 475, spanning the two columns, lists all the stated limitations, including absence of musical-experience ratings except discrete preference. Location and qualifies role are correct. The 25% overlap is the authors' reported figure; the unavailable Supporting Information was not used to recount tracks. Potential surrounding-statement effects: none identified for this anchor; the published correction and Supporting Information remain unchecked, and no inference about music versus silence or playlist efficacy follows from these limitations.

The principal reports and specified table rows are present. The original locator omitted the source of the review's explicit 25-study count (Abstract, p. 1), search update and addiction-treatment exclusion (Methods/Eligibility, p. 2); add these pages. The 16-music and 11-eye-mask counts are written out in the Session environment second paragraph on p. 9, with respectively 16 and 11 cited study entries when years are counted separately and the paired Carhart-Harris/Murphy report is treated as one study. Inspection of all Table 3 environment columns, pp. 11–15, finds exactly two explicit no-music entries, both on p. 13. The Carhart-Harris 2016 stereo-speaker discrepancy is correctly identified on p. 12; additional table nuance is that von Rotz permits headphones or speakers (p. 14), while Peck (p. 13) and Sloshower (p. 14) describe headphones/eye-shades as optional. Therefore retain the Results counts as review reports, not independently confirmed uniform actual use. Discussion paragraph 4 on p. 17 states the absence of efficacy comparisons across sets/settings; paragraph 5 discusses Kaelen as the music-experience relationship study. The narrowed statement about included studies is defensible as the review authors' report, not a freshly verified systematic absence finding. Role qualifies is appropriate. Potential surrounding-statement effects: retain attribution for the trial counts/procedures and the no-comparison conclusion; do not infer absence of music effects or generalize beyond this review's clinical/diagnostic scope. The supplied music statement already identifies the principal speaker discrepancy and the exclusion of substance-use treatment; the additional optional-use details refine limitations, without a rating change.
results.corrected_extracted: In a systematic review reporting 25 studies of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders (addiction-treatment studies excluded; searches updated on 6 December 2023), the Results text reports 16 studies playing a predefined music selection through headphones. Table 3, however, describes Carhart-Harris et al. (2016), one of those entries, with high-quality stereo speakers, von Rotz et al. (2023) with headphones or speakers, and headphones as optional in Peck et al. (2023) and Sloshower et al. (2023). The Results describes one study, Holze et al. (2023), alternating music and silence without headphones. Table 3 explicitly describes two studies with no music: dos Santos et al. (2021), where music and movies were not allowed, and D'Souza et al. (2022), with no music or decoration. The Results text reports 11 studies recommending an eye mask throughout; Table 3 describes eye-shades as optional in Peck and Sloshower. The Discussion states that no studies compared psychedelic efficacy in different sets and settings, and cites Kaelen et al. (2018) as specifically investigating the relationship between subjective music experience and psychedelic experience. These are descriptions and conclusions reported by the review, rather than primary-trial procedures independently checked here.
